purpose: Inputs for an ESTIMATE (not a measurement) of what a pedestrian breathes beside idling petrol scooters at a Taiwanese red light: exhaust speciation (benzene and other VOC), particle number, PM2.5 mass, and the CO-to-X emission ratios needed for a route that scales everything from CO.

verificationLevels.true: I opened the source (full text, table, or the legal text itself) in this session and found the figure in it.
verificationLevels.false: Not opened at full-text level. Level is spelled out in verificationLevel: abstract-only (abstract text retrieved via OpenAlex or a publisher page, figure is in the abstract), repo-extraction (taken from an earlier agent's full-text extraction under /home/user/scooterair/research, not re-opened by me), or unopened.

headline: Idle exhaust of a small four-stroke scooter, per kg of fuel burned: CO about 340 to 760 g/kg (Hanoi lab, Nepal workshop), hydrocarbons about 57 g/kg (Hanoi lab, a figure I derived from the Hanoi rate/fuel burn), BTEX about 15 g/kg in the Nepal workshop measurement. These all come from carburetted bikes without proven catalysts; a modern Taiwanese Phase 6/7 scooter should be well below them (Taiwan Tsai 2018 cycle-average CO is 84 g/L = about 114 g/kg for Phase V).

Benzene is a small slice of the hydrocarbons: Taiwan's own national inventory implies about 0.7% of motorcycle HC mass (286 t / 37,000 t, 2021, includes evaporative HC); the Nepal idle data imply about 2 to 6% if benzene is 20 to 35% of BTEX (assumption). Used range 0.7 to 6%, central about 2.5% (all assumption-labelled, see derived-benzene-share).

Ratios to CO by mass at idle: HC/CO about 0.08 to 0.33 (central about 0.17); benzene/CO about 0.3 to 1.0% (central about 0.5%, so CO:benzene about 100 to 350:1 by mass, 280 to 1000:1 by mole); PM2.5/CO 0.89 to 11.4 per mille (Nepal, serviced to unserviced); particle number about 1e10 to 3e11 per g CO (very weakly supported, see derived-pn-per-co).

PM2.5 at idle is the least certain and most skewed input: 0.71 g/kg (serviced) to 8.8 g/kg (unserviced) in the only idle measurement found, mostly lubricating oil; per-kg-fuel driving-cycle values for Euro 3 four-strokes are about 0.07 to 0.1 g/kg. Convert at 85 to 180 g fuel/h.

No source found gives a particle-number emission RATE at idle for any scooter (per second or per kg fuel). The only idle PN datum is a concentration in a Taiwanese lab dilution system (2.07e4 /cm3), which cannot be turned into a rate without the dilution ratio. Per-km values for four-strokes (2e11 to 3e12 /km, WMTC) are used to bracket a per-kg-fuel value instead.

Taiwan fuel limits: benzene 1.0% v/v max from 1 Jan 2012, 0.9% v/v max from 1 Jul 2020; aromatics 35% v/v, olefins 18% v/v. The Tsai test fuel had 0.52% benzene and 30% aromatics, so it is below the limit.

findings.claim: Taiwan's mobile-source fuel composition standard caps gasoline benzene at 1.0% v/v from 1 Jan 2012 (refinery) and 0.9% v/v from 1 Jul 2020 (refinery; imports too), with aromatics at 35% v/v and olefins at 18% v/v max. A third standard stage is dated 1 Jan 2024; its values were not readable.
findings.measured: Legal limits on commercial gasoline composition, Taiwan. Not a measurement.
findings.placeYear: Taiwan; standard issued 20 March 2020 (formerly Standard for Gasoline and Diesel Composition for Vehicles); stage dates 1 Jan 2012, 1 Jul 2020, 1 Jan 2024
findings.citation: Environmental Protection Administration (Executive Yuan), 移動污染源燃料成分管制標準 (Mobile Source Fuel Composition Control Standard), Art. 3 tables; text mirrored on 6laws.net, table values are embedded images that I read directly.
findings.url: https://6laws.net/6law/law3/移動污染源燃料成分管制標準.htm  (table images: https://6laws.net/6law/law3/law3images/移動污染源燃料成分管制標準/image003.png and image005.png)
findings.verificationLevel: read from the table images on an unofficial mirror of the regulation; not checked against the official gazette or the MOENV database page. image003 = first stage (benzene 1.0%, effective 1 Jan 2012 per its footnotes, 民國101年); image005 = second stage (benzene 0.9%, effective 1 Jul 2020, 民國109年). The third stage (1 Jan 2024) table image (image007) returned nothing.
findings.quote: image005: 苯含量 0.9% (v/v), 最大值; 硫含量 10 mg/kg; 蒸氣壓 60 kPa; 氧含量 2.7% (m/m); 芳香烴含量 35% (v/v); 烯烴含量 18% (v/v). image003: 苯含量 1.0% (v/v), 最大值 ...
findings.notes: Exhaust benzene comes from unburned fuel benzene plus formation from other aromatics, so fuel benzene sets a rough scale only. Tsai 2018 test fuel: 0.52% benzene, 30 vol% aromatics, 10.2% MTBE, so Taiwan retail 95 fuel is below the cap. MOENV 2024 third stage not confirmed; check the official page.

findings.claim: Exhaust VOC from 43 in-use Taiwanese four-stroke motorcycles (ECE cycle, 95-octane fuel with 0.52% benzene, 30 vol% aromatics) was 38-48% aromatics, 38-45% paraffins, 9.7-15% olefins, 1.8-3.0% carbonyls by mass, with total VOC 25.2 g/L fuel (5,231 km) to 47.1 g/L (47,617 km). Benzene is named among the main VOCs, but its own value is not in the abstract.
findings.unit: g per litre of fuel burned; % of VOC mass
findings.measured: Chassis dynamometer, whole ECE cycle (780 s, 240 s idle), 43 four-stroke motorcycles, 52 VOC + 15 carbonyls; not idle-only, not scooter-specific.
findings.citation: Chiang H.-L. et al. (Tsai group), Fuel Economy and Volatile Organic Compound Exhaust Emission for Motorcycles with Various Running Mileages. Aerosol and Air Quality Research 18(12), 2018. doi:10.4209/aaqr.2018.07.0264
findings.verificationLevel: abstract (checked here via OpenAlex) plus repo-extraction (/home/user/scooterair/research/papers/tsai-2018-aaqr.json, which records a full-text read). The aaqr.org PDF returned HTTP 403 to me, so I did not open it.
findings.quote: Abstract: 'The exhaust of VOC groups profiled included paraffins (38-45%), olefins (9.7-15%), aromatics (38-48%), and carbonyls (1.8-3.0%) ... Toluene, isopentane, m,p-xylene, o-xylene, 1-butene, 1,2,4-trimethylbenzene, ethylbenzene, n-pentane, and benzene were the main VOCs in motorcycle exhaust.'
findings.notes: Whole-cycle ECE, so cold-start and driving are mixed in; idle is 31% of cycle time but results are not separated. Benzene mass per litre and per cent of VOC would be in the full text (Table 2); fetch manually. Convert g/L to g/kg with gasoline density 0.74 kg/L (assumption, 0.72-0.77). The 25.2 vs 19.1 g/L low-mileage inconsistency in the paper is noted in the repo extraction.

findings.claim: In 40 Taiwanese four-stroke motorcycles, Phase V total VOC was 0.59 g/km (lowest), and BTEX fell 37-58% (Phase IV) and 44-62% (Phase V) relative to Phase III. VOC group fractions were similar across phases.
findings.measured: Chassis dynamometer, ECE cycle, 40 four-stroke motorcycles of Phases III-V.
findings.citation: Yao Y.-C., Tsai J.-H., Chiang H.-L. et al., Criteria Pollutants and Volatile Organic Compounds Emitted from Motorcycle Exhaust under Various Regulation Phases. Aerosol and Air Quality Research 17, 2017. doi:10.4209/aaqr.2016.04.0155
findings.verificationLevel: abstract only (via OpenAlex); aaqr.org PDF returned HTTP 403. Author list is as I recall it and should be checked; the repo's own entry cites the same DOI as 'Tsai 2017'.
findings.quote: 'The total VOC emissions of Phase V motorcycles were the lowest (0.59 g km-1) ... the fraction of VOC groups was similar among all test motorcycles regardless of different regulation phases. ... BTEX decreased by 37-58% and 44-62%, respectively, for Phases IV and V motorcycles compared to those of Phase III.'
findings.notes: Useful as a scaling: Phase V is about 0.4x the CO and 0.57x the HC of Phase III and BTEX is about 0.4-0.55x. Taiwanese scooters at a kerb are a mix of Phase III-VII; a Phase VI/VII scooter (Euro 4/5 equivalent) is cleaner again but no Taiwanese speciation exists for it.

findings.claim: A Taiwanese dynamometer survey of new and in-use 2- and 4-stroke Phase III motorcycles sampled idle among the driving stages. For four-strokes, VOC emission factors were 344 mg/km (new) and 433 mg/km (in-use); dominant VOC were isopentane (295 mg/km), 2-methylpentane (83), 3-methylpentane (66) and toluene (100 mg/km). Carbonyls were 3.1 (new) and 4.6 (in-use) mg/km; formaldehyde 0.4 / 0.7 and acetaldehyde 0.6 / 1.2 mg/km (new / in-use, 2- and 4-stroke pooled as printed).
findings.measured: Chassis dynamometer, ECE cycle with stage-resolved samples (idle, acceleration, 30 and 50 km/h cruise, deceleration), 10 new and 15 in-use Phase III motorcycles, Tedlar bag GC.
findings.citation: Tsai J.-H., Chiang H.-L. et al., Volatile Organic Profiles and Photochemical Potentials from Motorcycle Engine Exhaust. Journal of the Air & Waste Management Association 53, 2003. doi:10.1080/10473289.2003.10466199
findings.verificationLevel: abstract only (via OpenAlex); the Taylor & Francis PDF was not opened. Authors/year taken from the DOI record; verify before citing.
findings.quote: 'The dominant volatile organic carbon (VOC) species were isopentane (53 and 295 mg/km, 2- and 4-stroke, respectively), 2-methylpentane (75 and 83 mg/km), 3-methylpentane (34 and 66 mg/km), and toluene (30 and 100 mg/km). The VOC emission factors for the 2-/4-stroke motorcycles were 311/344 (new) and 1479/433 (in-use) mg/km'
findings.notes: Phase III is the oldest Taiwanese four-stroke phase; benzene is not listed among the dominant species in the abstract. Toluene is about 23% of in-use four-stroke VOC mass (100/433, my division). The idle-stage speciation is in the full text and would be the best Taiwanese idle benzene figure; it should be fetched manually. Two-stroke in-use VOC is 3.4x the four-stroke.

findings.claim: Taiwan's national inventory (TEDS-based, 2021) implies motorcycle benzene is about 0.77% of motorcycle hydrocarbon mass (286 t benzene / 37,000 t HC), and about 1.5% in 2013 (1,048 t / 68,000 t) when two-strokes were a bigger share. The HC total includes evaporative HC; benzene exhaust factor comes from dynamometer data.
findings.measured: Modelled national inventory, not a measurement. Ratio is my division of two printed totals.
findings.citation: Tsai J.-H.; Chen J.-Y.; Chiang H.-L. Airborne Air Pollutant Emission Characteristics of Mobile Vehicles in Taiwan. Atmosphere 14(6), 916, 2023. doi:10.3390/atmos14060916
findings.verificationLevel: repo-extraction (/home/user/scooterair/research/papers/tsai-2023-atmosphere.json, full-text read, findings benzene-totals and hc-totals). Not re-opened; MDPI returned 403 to me on a different paper.
findings.notes: The lowest benzene/HC ratio available for Taiwan; likely biased low as a share of EXHAUST HC because evaporative HC (low benzene share per the paper's own text) is in the denominator, and because inventory emission factors are for well-maintained test vehicles. Use as the low end of the benzene fraction range. The paper states motorcycle benzene EF is higher than gasoline cars per km but prints no value.

findings.claim: Five four-stroke carburetted motorcycles and one scooter, sampled at start-up and idling in Kathmandu, emitted per kg of fuel burned: CO 710 g/kg (SD 389; pre-service fleet) and 761 (SD 327; post-service), ethylene 13.2, acetylene 11.7, BTEX about 15 g/kg, 1,3-butadiene 1.30 (SD 0.51) g/kg, formaldehyde 0.548 g/kg. Aromatics were about 31% of NMHC, toluene the most abundant aromatic.
findings.measured: FTIR at the tailpipe (about 1 m downstream of manifold for generators; motorcycles sampled at tailpipe) for CO/CH4/C2H4/etc.; whole-air canister (GC) for BTEX and aromatic fraction from ONE motorcycle pre-service. Start-up and idle, not driving.
findings.placeYear: Kathmandu, Nepal, 13 April 2015; four-stroke Indian-built bikes, 3-15 years old, no catalytic converters assumed (required in India for four-strokes only from 2015)
findings.citation: Stockwell C.E. et al., Nepal Ambient Monitoring and Source Testing Experiment (NAMaSTE): emissions of trace gases and light-absorbing carbon from wood and dung cooking fires, garbage and crop residue burning, brick kilns, and other sources. Atmospheric Chemistry and Physics 16, 11043-11081, 2016. doi:10.5194/acp-16-11043-2016
findings.verificationLevel: full text downloaded and read (open access, CC BY 3.0). Table 1 (fleet averages) and Sect. 3.2. Supplement Table S4 (per-bike values, WAS speciation incl. benzene alone) NOT available to me.
findings.quote: Sect. 3.2: 'the FTIR-measured average EFs pre- and post-service over 700 g kg-1'; 'the next most abundant emissions after CO were C2 hydrocarbons (~24 g kg-1), BTEX (benzene, toluene, ethylbenzene, and xylenes) compounds (~15 g kg-1)'; 'The BTEX and acetone data are from the one motorcycle that was analyzed by WAS pre-service'; 'aromatics account for ~31% of the NMHC in the exhaust emissions, with toluene being the most abundant aromatic'; 'high emissions of 1,3-butadiene (~1.3 g kg-1)'. Table 1: CO 710 (389) / 761 (327); HCHO 0.548 / 0.535; 1,3-butadiene 1.30 (0.51) / 1.19 (0.56).
findings.notes: BEST available idle speciation but weak applicability: old, unserviced, carburetted bikes with MCE 0.6 (CO/CO2 molar about 0.66, extremely rich). Taiwanese scooters (CVT, mostly Phase V+ with catalysts and, increasingly, fuel injection) should be far cleaner; Taiwan's Phase III cycle-average CO is about 290 g/kg. Treat Nepal as a high bound for a bad old carburetted scooter. BTEX value is one bike, not a fleet. Benzene alone is not in the main text. Authors say their ratios to CO for benzene etc. were only 3-26% of Hanoi IVE start-up/running ratios (Oanh 2012), except 1,3-butadiene.

findings.claim: Five Hanoi motorcycle models at steady idle (laboratory) emitted CO 60.9, HC 10.3, NOx 1.8 g/h burning about 180 g fuel/h; a second Vietnamese test of 15 motorcycles measured idle fuel 0.141 g per 5 s and 0.703 g per 30 s (about 85-100 g/h).
findings.measured: Laboratory idle, five Hanoi motorcycle models; second paper 15 motorcycles idle fuel.
findings.citation: Nguyen et al., Int. J. of Urban Sciences (2021), doi:10.1080/12265934.2020.1871059; Nguyen et al., J. Chinese Institute of Engineers (2025), doi:10.1080/02533839.2025.2531199
findings.verificationLevel: repo-extraction (/home/user/scooterair/research/redlight/idle-emissions.json, findings nguyen-2021-hanoi-idle and nguyen-2025-idle-vs-restart, marked VERIFIED by an earlier agent). Not re-opened by me. The 84 g/h figure is my division of 0.703 g/30 s.
findings.quote: Repo extraction: 'Steady idle: CO 60.9, HC 10.3, NOx 1.8, CO2 534.3 g/h; fuel about 180 g/h.'
findings.notes: Not Taiwanese scooters. Provides the idle HC/CO and CO per kg fuel that the Nepal numbers cross-check: Nepal CO 710 g/kg vs Hanoi 338 g/kg; Hanoi HC 57 g/kg is close to the 57 g/kg NMHC I back out of the Nepal BTEX (15 g/kg / (0.31 aromatics fraction x 0.85 BTEX share)). Idle fuel burn range 85-180 g/h is the key conversion for PM and PN.

findings.claim: Taiwan's idle-test limits, converted to a mass rate, imply about 40 g CO/h at the 2.0% limit and about 90 g CO/h at the 4.5% limit for a scooter burning 130 g fuel/h.
findings.measured: Derived by me. Working: exhaust mass flow = fuel 0.130 kg/h x (1 + AFR 14.7) = 2.04 kg/h = 70 mol/h at MW 29; CO = 2.0% x 70 mol/h = 1.4 mol/h x 28 g/mol = 39 g/h; 4.5% gives 88 g/h.
findings.citation: MOENV Standards for Air Pollutant Emissions from Mobile Sources, Art. 6, Executive Yuan Gazette vol. 29 no. 121 (30 June 2023)
findings.verificationLevel: limits themselves are repo-extraction (idle-emissions.json, moenv-idle-limits-inuse, VERIFIED by an earlier agent); the conversion is mine and rests on assumptions: AFR 14.7 (stoichiometric), idle fuel 130 g/h, CO reported on a dry, volume basis.
findings.quote: n/a (derived)
findings.notes: Cross-check only: the legal limit corresponds to 40-90 g CO/h, the same order as the Hanoi measurement of 61 g/h. Real idle exhaust of a failing scooter can exceed the limit. 94-96% of Taiwanese scooters pass inspection, so most idle below the limit, but the limit is also the permitted value, not typical.

findings.claim: Five idling four-stroke carburetted motorcycles in Kathmandu emitted PM2.5 of 8.81 +/- 1.33 g/kg fuel before servicing and 0.71 +/- 0.45 g/kg after an oil change, air-filter and spark-plug cleaning and carburettor adjustment. The reduction was mainly lubricating oil: OC fell from 7.21 to 0.02 g/kg while EC stayed 0.39 to 0.31 g/kg. PM2.5:CO was 11.4 per mille before and 0.89 per mille after.
findings.unit: g/kg fuel; per mille; mg/h (derived: g/kg x 0.085 to 0.180 kg/h)
findings.measured: Filter sample composite of five bikes, each about 10 min at idle, onto one filter; undiluted-style field sampling (not CVS); PM2.5 by filter, speciated OC/EC/ions/PAH/hopanes.
findings.citation: Jayarathne T. et al., Nepal Ambient Monitoring and Source Testing Experiment (NAMaSTE): emissions of particulate matter from wood- and dung-fueled cooking fires, garbage and crop residue burning, brick kilns, and other sources. Atmospheric Chemistry and Physics 18, 2259-2286, 2018. doi:10.5194/acp-18-2259-2018
findings.verificationLevel: full text downloaded and read (open access). Sect. 3.6 and Table 1.
findings.quote: 'EFPM2.5 was 8.81 +/- 1.33 g kg-1 before servicing and dropped considerably to 0.71 +/- 0.45 g kg-1 after servicing (Fig. 3c). OC, the major chemical component of emissions before servicing, dropped from 7.21 to 0.02 g kg-1 after servicing.' 'The ratio of PM2.5 : CO (wt / wt) was 11.4 per mille before servicing and 0.89 per mille after servicing.' Authors state the data are 'neither representative of the diverse Kathmandu vehicle fleet nor their integrated emissions'.
findings.notes: Only idle PM2.5 mass measurement found for a four-stroke motorcycle; the authors call it unrepresentative. Four models (Honda Hero CBZ, Hero Splendor, Aviator, Bajaj Pulsar), 3-15 years old, carburetted. High unserviced value is dominated by crankcase oil mist and probably semi-volatile condensate; a modern Taiwanese fuel-injected scooter with a catalyst and PCV should be at or below the serviced value. The serviced 0.71 g/kg is still 7-10x the per-kg-fuel driving-cycle PM of Euro 3 motorcycles (see kontses-pm-and-pn).

findings.claim: Euro 3-4 four-stroke motorcycles over the WMTC emitted solid particles >23 nm (SPN23) of 2e11 to 20e11 per km (average 1.1-1.6x the 6e11/km Euro 6 car limit), four-stroke carburetted mopeds about 11e11 per km, and two-stroke mopeds about 11x the car limit (about 6.6e12/km; up to 4.5e13/km across the L-category set). Motorcycle PM was 0.6-2.2 mg/km (Euro 3, other studies cited) and about 1.5 mg/km (Costagliola 2016, cited); geometric mean particle size 20.9-35.7 nm on five vehicles; counting down to 10 nm adds 25-67% (up to 2.4x for quads).
findings.measured: Chassis dynamometer, WMTC (600 s cold phase + hot phase), CVS with solid-particle counter (23 nm cut, catalytic stripper style, PMP protocol), 4S/2S mopeds, motorcycles (mostly port-fuel-injected, two carburetted 15/16), quads, minicars. No idle data.
findings.placeYear: European laboratory (JRC Ispra / Aristotle University), vehicles Euro 1-4; published 2020
findings.citation: Kontses A., Ntziachristos L., Zardini A.A., Papadopoulos G., Giechaskiel B. Particulate emissions from L-category vehicles towards Euro 5. Environmental Research 182, 109071, 2020. doi:10.1016/j.envres.2019.109071
findings.verificationLevel: full text downloaded (Europe PMC XML) and searched. The per-km values for individual sub-categories are given in the paper mostly as multiples of the 6e11/km limit (figure/text), so the absolute numbers above are my multiplications of the printed multiples; the text numbers 11e11, 2S 'about 11 times' and 'up to 5 times' are quoted directly.
findings.quote: 'Emission levels of 4S mopeds over WMTC (11 x 10^11 km-1) are consistent to the study performed by Favre et al. (2011) on Euro 3 vehicles.' 'SPN23 emissions from these sub-categories were up to 5 times higher than the Euro 6 passenger cars limit (6 x 10^11 km-1). Even recent Euro 4 motorcycles exceeded this limit by up to 3 times.' 'GMD ... varies among the different vehicles in the range between 20.9 and 35.7 nm.' 'In the other sub-categories, SPN10 emissions were 25-67% higher than SPN23 emissions.' 'Motorcycle PM ... Favre et al. (2009) evaluated 4 Euro 3 motorcycles and exhibited emissions in the range of 0.6-2.2 mg/km.'
findings.notes: Per-km, driving-cycle, European and mostly fuel-injected: no idle information, no Taiwanese vehicles. Taiwan Phase 5 = Euro 3 equivalent, Phase 6 = Euro 4. Particle size is small (about 20-35 nm), so most numbers sit in the nucleation/ultrafine range and decay fast with distance by coagulation and dilution. At roughly 41-47 km per kg of fuel (34.7 km/L / 0.74 kg/L), 2e11-2e12 per km becomes about 0.8e13-9e13 per kg fuel.

findings.claim: Euro 1 and Euro 2 two-stroke 50 cc scooters emitted particle number of order 1e13 per km (gasoline car 1e12, diesel 1e14), organic aerosol 30-472 mg/km, BC 0.14-1.15 mg/km, HC 11-36x the other vehicles, aromatics 99-211 mg/km, with benzene/toluene ratios of 0.24-0.90 and raw benzene at idle as high as 146 ppm.
findings.unit: per km; mg/km; ratio; ppm; g/kg
findings.measured: Chassis dynamometer (ECE47, WMTC) and smog-chamber idling tests, 2 two-stroke scooters (Euro 1 carburetted with oxidation catalyst; Euro 2 with secondary air and oxidation catalyst) in Chirico; 3 in Platt.
findings.citation: (a) Chirico R. et al., Emissions of organic aerosol mass, black carbon, particle number, and regulated and unregulated gases from scooters and light and heavy duty vehicles with different fuels, Atmospheric Chemistry and Physics Discussions 14, 16591-16639, 2014 (discussion paper; final version ACP 14, 2014, check). doi:10.5194/acpd-14-16591-2014. (b) Platt S.M. et al., Two-stroke scooters are a dominant source of air pollution in many cities, Nature Communications 5, 3749, 2014. doi:10.1038/ncomms4749
findings.verificationLevel: both full texts downloaded and read. Chirico is the discussion (pre-review) version. Platt Supplementary Tables 2 and 3 (idle EFs) not available to me. The 10-100 g/kg BTEX range is quoted second-hand from Stockwell 2016 describing Platt.
findings.quote: Chirico: 'those of the scooters were in the order of 10^13 km-1'; 'The organic aerosol mass emissions ... 30-472 mg km-1 for the scooters'; 'The scooters featured the highest emissions of aromatic compounds (99-211 mg km-1)'; 'The average benzene/toluene values ... 0.24-0.90 for the scooters'; 'the EF(HC) for scooters were 11-36 times higher'. Platt: 'toxic aromatic emissions (up to ~40% of emitted VOC volume ...) ... Levels in the raw 2S scooter exhaust were as high as 300,000 ug m-3 or 146 p.p.m.(v) from idling.'
findings.notes: Two-stroke only. Taiwan has about 280,000 registered two-strokes (about 2% of the fleet, repo idle-emissions.json) but Tsai 2023 implies they produce a disproportionate share of motorcycle HC and benzene. Their presence in a queue would raise local aromatics and organic aerosol strongly; the number per red light is unknown. 'Scooter' in these papers means 50 cc two-stroke mopeds, not the 4-stroke 125 cc CVT scooter that dominates Taiwan. Benzene/toluene of 0.24-0.90 is the only benzene-to-toluene ratio for any scooter found; it is used to bound benzene as a fraction of BTEX.

findings.claim: One Taiwanese four-stroke motorcycle gave total particle number concentrations of 2.07e4, 2.35e4 and 2.60e4 per cm3 at idle, 15 km/h and 30 km/h in a laboratory dilution system, and about 80% of the emitted particles were inhalable (the rest of that sentence is truncated in the abstract). Idle number was 80% of the 30 km/h value.
findings.unit: particles per cm3 (diluted, in the sampling train)
findings.measured: Size-resolved particle number and particle-bound PAH from one 95-octane four-stroke motorcycle on a dynamometer at idle, 15 and 30 km/h; dilution ratio not stated in the abstract.
findings.citation: Chien S.-M., Huang Y.-J. (and coauthors), Sizes and polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbon composition distributions of nano, ultrafine, fine, and coarse particulates emitted from a four-stroke motorcycle. Journal of Environmental Science and Health, Part A 45(13), 2010. doi:10.1080/10934529.2010.513289
findings.verificationLevel: abstract only (via OpenAlex); the Taylor & Francis page returned HTTP 403, so the full text, the dilution ratio and the size distribution were not seen. Author names as in the repo entry (chien-huang-2010-idle-pn).
findings.quote: 'The particle total number concentrations (TNCs) emitted while idling and at 15 and 30 km/h were 2.07 x 10^4, 2.35 x 10^4, and 2.60 x 10^4 #/cm3, respectively; i.e., they increased at elevated speeds.'
findings.notes: Cannot be converted to a rate without dilution ratio and flow. Its value for the estimate is the SHAPE: idle PN is of the same order as at 15-30 km/h (0.8x), so using the driving-cycle per-km values to bracket idle per kg fuel is not wildly wrong for a four-stroke. A search summary I could not confirm (a Taiwanese sampling-system thesis, NCU repository, host did not resolve) quotes idle at 1750 rpm with count median diameter 0.05 um, GSD 1.8 and 1e4-1e5 per cm3: unverified, not used.

findings.claim: Four large in-use motorcycles (599-1078 cc) emitted 2.6e10 to 2.7e11 non-volatile particles per km, with 29-75% of particles below 23 nm.
findings.measured: In-use regulated and unregulated emissions with flow measurement, four large motorcycles.
findings.citation: Pechout M. et al., Atmospheric Environment: X 2022, doi:10.1016/j.aeaoa.2022.100170
findings.verificationLevel: repo-extraction (idle-emissions.json, pechout-2022-large-motorcycles). The ScienceDirect PDF returned HTTP 403 to me.
findings.quote: Repo: 'Particles 2.6e10-2.7e11 /km; 29-75% under 23 nm'.
findings.notes: Large, modern, fuel-injected touring-class bikes; the low end of the per-km range, not scooters. Shows the PN range spans a factor of about 10 across four-stroke engine types.

findings.claim: Idle CO per kg of fuel for small four-strokes is about 340 g/kg (Hanoi lab) to 710-760 g/kg (Nepal workshop). A Taiwanese cycle-average CO is 114 g/kg (Phase V, 84.3 g/L) to 292 g/kg (Phase III, 216 g/L). Taiwanese scooters in good order at idle are probably between about 100 and 400 g/kg.
findings.measured: Derived. Tsai g/L converted with gasoline density 0.74 kg/L (assumption, 0.72-0.77).
findings.citation: Derived from nguyen-2021-hanoi-idle (secondary), nepal-idle-speciation (verified), tsai-2018 (abstract/repo)
findings.verificationLevel: derived; low/central/high for Taiwan are ASSUMPTIONS (basis: modern-catalyst scooters idle richer than cycle average because the catalyst is cooler and AFR control is open-loop at idle; Taiwan idle limit of 2% CO corresponds to about 40 g/h at 130 g/h fuel = about 300 g/kg).
findings.quote: n/a
findings.notes: Central 250 g/kg x 130 g fuel/h = about 33 g CO/h per scooter; range 100 x 85 = 8.5 g/h up to 400 x 180 = 72 g/h. Compare Hanoi measured 61 g/h and the legal limit 40-90 g/h.

findings.claim: Benzene is about 0.7% (Taiwan inventory) to about 6% (Nepal idle, with an assumed benzene share of BTEX) of exhaust hydrocarbon mass, central about 2.5%. Per kg of fuel at idle this is roughly 0.4 to 3.4 g/kg; per hour 0.04 to 0.6 g/h per scooter.
findings.unit: % of HC mass; g/kg fuel; g/h
findings.measured: Derived. Working (Nepal route): NMHC = BTEX 15 g/kg / (aromatics 0.31 x BTEX share of aromatics 0.85) = 57 g/kg, which matches Hanoi HC 57 g/kg. Benzene = ASSUMED 20-35% of BTEX (basis: benzene/toluene 0.24-0.90 in two-stroke scooters (Chirico), toluene is the most abundant aromatic (Stockwell, Tsai 2018)); 15 x 0.20 = 3.0 and 15 x 0.35 = 5.3 g/kg, or 5-9% of 57 g/kg; the high end here is 6% after allowing for the Nepal bikes' extreme richness. Low end: Taiwan inventory 0.77% x 57 g/kg = 0.44 g/kg. Per hour: 0.4-3.4 g/kg x 0.085-0.180 kg/h = 0.03-0.6 g/h; central 1.4 g/kg x 0.130 = 0.18 g/h.
findings.citation: Derived from nepal-idle-speciation, hanoi-idle-rates-from-repo, tsai-2023-benzene-share-of-hc-inventory, chirico-2s-scooter-pn-pm-voc
findings.verificationLevel: derived and assumption-based; the benzene fraction of BTEX (20-35%) and the central 2.5% are ASSUMPTIONS. No source I could open gives the benzene mass fraction of four-stroke scooter exhaust directly: Tsai 2017/2018 would (aaqr.org 403) and Stockwell Table S4 would.
findings.quote: n/a
findings.notes: Cross-check: if benzene is about 1% of fuel mass (Taiwan cap 0.9% v/v, roughly 0.9% by mass), 1.4 g/kg fuel is about 14% of fuel benzene surviving unburnt or reforming, plausible for a rich idle. Benzene is quoted as 'the' hazardous component for the site, so this is the weakest link between CO and benzene: a factor of 8 spread.

findings.claim: Emission ratios implied for scaling from CO at idle (mass basis): HC/CO 0.08-0.33 (central 0.17); benzene/CO 0.3-1.0% (central 0.5%); BTEX/CO 2.1% (Nepal); 1,3-butadiene/CO 0.18% (Nepal); formaldehyde/CO 0.08% (Nepal); PM2.5/CO 0.089-1.14% (Nepal, serviced to unserviced).

values.HC_over_CO_basis: Nepal 57/710 = 0.08; Hanoi 10.3/60.9 = 0.17; Tsai Phase III 54/216 = 0.25 and Phase V 29.4/84.3 = 0.35 (cycle average, g/L basis)
values.benzene_over_CO_basis: benzene g/kg from derived-benzene-share divided by CO g/kg: central 1.4/250 = 0.56%; high 3.4/340 = 1.0%; extreme low 0.4/710 = 0.06% (see notes)

findings.measured: Derived from the findings listed above.
findings.citation: See component findings.
findings.verificationLevel: derived; HC/CO and PM2.5/CO come straight from measurements (Hanoi lab, Nepal workshop, Tsai whole-cycle); the benzene/CO ratio rests on the assumption-based benzene share.
findings.quote: n/a
findings.notes: The low end of benzene/CO combines the lowest benzene share (0.7%) with the highest CO (Nepal): 0.4 g/kg / 710 g/kg = 0.06%; the 0.3% low end quoted above uses mid CO (340 g/kg) and is therefore not the extreme. Honest full range of benzene/CO by mass is about 0.06% to 1.0% (factor 17), central about 0.5%. Ratios are for idle: benzene/CO at cruise differs, since the catalyst converts HC and CO differently (Zhang 1995, quoted in Stockwell 2016, that partly working catalysts lower VOC/CO).

findings.claim: Particle number per kg of fuel for four-strokes is bracketed at about 1e13 to 1.4e14 per kg (central about 5e13 per kg) from WMTC per-km values and Taiwanese fuel economy. Per gram of CO this is about 1e10 to 3e11 (central about 2e11), assuming idle PN per kg fuel is of the same order as at 15-30 km/h (supported by Chien & Huang idle = 0.8x 30 km/h).

values.two_stroke_PN_per_s_central_note: 1e13/km x 47 km/kg x 0.130/3600 = about 1.7e10/s (about 10x the four-stroke central)

findings.unit: particles per kg fuel; per s; per g CO
findings.measured: Derived. Working: PN/kg = PN/km x km/kg; 1.1e12 x 46.9 = 5.2e13; per second at 130 g/h = 5.2e13 x 0.130 / 3600 = 1.9e9 /s. PN/g CO = 5.2e13 / 250 g CO per kg = 2.1e11.
findings.citation: Derived from kontses-pm-and-pn (verified, European four-strokes) and tsai-2018 fuel economy (abstract); idle-versus-driving argument from chien-huang-2010 (abstract).
findings.verificationLevel: derived. Weakest particle input: no idle PN rate exists for any scooter. Assumptions: (1) idle PN per kg of fuel is within a factor of 3 of the WMTC average per kg of fuel, (2) Taiwanese scooters behave like Euro 3-4 European four-strokes, (3) density 0.74. Plausible range is a factor of about 15 either side because Taiwanese carburetted older scooters and oil-burning could be far higher (Nepal organic aerosol) and fuel-injected catalyst scooters lower (Pechout 2.6e10/km, 20x lower).
findings.quote: n/a
findings.notes: Solid particle number above 23 nm; total number including volatile nucleation mode and 10-23 nm would be roughly 1.3-2x higher (SPN10/SPN23 1.25-1.67), and more for 'real dilution' conditions where semi-volatile material condenses (Kontses). Size is small (GMD about 20-35 nm), so number decays quickly over metres to tens of metres.

findings.claim: PM2.5 mass rate at idle per scooter: about 13-18 mg/h (0.07-0.1 g/kg, driving-cycle Euro 3 scaled to fuel) through 60-130 mg/h (Nepal serviced 0.71 g/kg) to 1.6 g/h (Nepal unserviced 8.8 g/kg). Central assumption 0.3 g/kg x 130 g/h = about 40 mg/h.
findings.measured: Derived. Low end 0.07 g/kg x 0.085 kg/h = 6 mg/h; central 0.3 x 0.130 = 39 mg/h; high 0.71 x 0.180 = 128 mg/h; extreme 8.81 x 0.180 = 1586 mg/h.
findings.citation: Derived from nepal-idle-pm25 (verified) and kontses-pm-and-pn (verified).
findings.verificationLevel: derived; the central 0.3 g/kg is an ASSUMPTION (geometric-ish midpoint between driving-cycle 0.07 and serviced idle 0.71, basis: idle PM per kg fuel exceeds cruising PM because of oil and rich operation). The weakest mass input; spread is a factor of 20 within 'sensible' and 200 including unserviced oil burners.
findings.quote: n/a
findings.notes: PM2.5 from a handful of scooters is small beside regional PM2.5 (Taiwan ambient about 10-20 ug/m3); this source is likely to be most visible through number concentration and organics, not mass. Taiwan inventory: motorcycles are 1.3% of primary PM2.5 (repo digest).

findings.claim: Formaldehyde and acetaldehyde from four-stroke motorcycles are small: Tsai 2018 carbonyls 0.41-0.80 g/L fuel (1.8-3.0% of VOC mass; formaldehyde 0.47-1.18 g/L, acetaldehyde 0.58-0.97 g/L per the repo extraction), Tsai 2003 formaldehyde 0.4-0.7 and acetaldehyde 0.6-1.2 mg/km; Nepal idle formaldehyde 0.55 g/kg and 1,3-butadiene 1.3 g/kg. 1,3-butadiene has no Taiwanese motorcycle value.
findings.measured: See component sources (dynamometer ECE cycle for Tsai; idle FTIR for Nepal).
findings.verificationLevel: mixed: Nepal values verified in full text; Tsai 2018 per-species values are repo-extraction; Tsai 2003 abstract only; Tsai 2023 repo-extraction. Row marked false because most of it is not full-text verified by me.
findings.quote: Nepal Table 1: 'Formaldehyde (HCHO) 0.548 / 0.535; 1,3-Butadiene (C4H6) 1.30 (0.51) / 1.19 (0.56)'.
findings.notes: Ratio to benzene: Nepal 1,3-butadiene is about the same order as benzene (1.3 vs about 1.4 g/kg central); formaldehyde about 0.4 of benzene. Not needed for the headline chart; useful as secondary toxics. Nepal note: only the scooter produced detectable formaldehyde on FTIR.

findings.claim: Two non-tailpipe contributions can matter at a kerb and are outside the tailpipe numbers: evaporative HC (Taiwan limit 2 g/test 1991; 2000 mg/test 2017; 1500 mg/test 2021) and crankcase oil mist (Nepal OC 7.2 g/kg unserviced).

bestEstimatesForModel.note: Everything below is for ONE idling four-stroke scooter in reasonable condition; it is an ESTIMATE built from derived findings. 'Assumption' marks values whose central value is my choice, not a measurement. Fuel burn at idle: 85-180 g/h, central 130 g/h (Hanoi 180; second Vietnamese test about 84-100).

holes: No Taiwanese idle emission rate for any scooter, and no benzene mass fraction of four-stroke scooter exhaust that I could open (the Tsai 2017 and 2018 PDFs on aaqr.org returned 403; Stockwell's per-bike speciation is in a supplement).

No particle NUMBER emission rate at idle (per second or per kg fuel) for any small four-stroke; the only idle datum is a diluted concentration (Chien & Huang 2010) with the dilution ratio unseen. The per-kg-fuel value is bracketed from WMTC per-km values (European, mostly injected).
No idle PM2.5 measurement for a Taiwanese scooter; the only idle PM2.5 number is five old carburetted Nepali bikes (0.71-8.8 g/kg), dominated by oil, and the authors call it unrepresentative.
Fuel-injected versus carburetted idle emission rates: no study found that separates them at idle. Taiwan's current scooter fleet by fuel system (carburettor versus injection) was not looked up.
Phase VI and VII (Euro 4/5-equivalent) Taiwanese scooters have no published speciation; Tsai 2017/2018 cover Phases III-V only.
Idle versus driving VOC speciation: Tsai 2003 sampled the idle stage but the stage-resolved benzene figures are in the full text only.

The proportion of scooters at a Taiwanese red light that are two-strokes or high-emitters is unknown; two-strokes emit 3.4x the VOC in-use (Tsai 2003) and 11-36x the HC of cars (Chirico), organic aerosol orders of magnitude higher.
Third-stage fuel limits from 1 Jan 2024 (benzene value) were not readable; the 0.9% v/v 2020 stage is the last one I confirmed, from an unofficial mirror.
The 1,3-butadiene share was not measured in any Taiwanese motorcycle study I could open.
Dhital et al. 2019 (carburettor versus fuel-injected engine-dynamometer VOC, catalyst effect on BTEX 88%) turned up only in a search summary; I could not locate or open the paper and did not use it.
